text: Cassini had to smash into Saturn because its tanks and electronics carry trace microbes from Earth. If it drifted into Enceladus or Titan, a small chance of cross-contaminating life there scared the mission planners. Sending it into orbit wasn’t safe either—gravity from Saturn and its big moons would eventually toss the probe somewhere unexpected. Crashing it into the planet was the fail-safe way to make sure the craft stayed out of reach of the interesting moons. The dive was timed so that Saturn’s gravity swallowed it up.

Ha, the standing leg thing. The stationary leg is working way harder than most people expect. When you're riding, your board leg does the pumping and balancing, but your stationary leg has to hold the angle that lets your board stay flat. If your stance is too narrow, that standing leg gets overworked, and the adductor group on the inside of the thigh and the hip flexor up near the groin are the ones taking most of the strain. I'm no medical guy, but iirc when folks complain of that side hurting, its usually because the leg is locked up instead of kept loose.

You might also be dragging that foot a little, or catching your toe on the pavement, which will make the inside of the ankle and the sole ache. And if you're on a board with a long wheelbase, the standing leg has to fight the torque more, especially when you do manual moves or even just keep the board level. Dealers love that trick of selling wide, stable longboards and then folks wonder why their legs feel dead after a session.

I guess the fix is mostly form. Keep the standing leg bent a bit and active, not stiff. Rotate your shoulders so your body is facing the board a little instead of being perfectly sideways to it. If the pain is sharp, stop and stretch the hip flexor and adductor gently. Its not about pushing through it. And if you just started skating, give your muscles a few weeks; the stationary leg is basically a stabilizer that most people don't train on purpose.

No, it’s not meant to imply everyone came from Africa in the last year. The “Afro-” part is shorthand for ancestry. Most Black Americans trace some family back to West, Central, or West-Central Africa, even though they’ve lived in the US for generations, so it’s an identity and heritage label, not a migration record.

As far as I know, this naming started picking up in the 1970s and “African American” and “Black American” get mixed together all the time. I could be wrong on the exact dating of the term, but the core idea is ancestry, not where your parents or grandparents were born. Some people don’t like the label at all, and some do, and that’s the main split you’ll hear in the conversation.

Honestly, if someone tells you “African American” means their whole family is currently in Lagos, that’s not how most people mean it. It’s closer to “has African roots.”

No, at least as far as I know there isnt one out there. The same parts of the brain that make a hit feel euphoric are the same ones your body starts to compensate around, so the pleasure and the damage ride along together. When someone gets high, the neurons are flooded with whatever chemical the drug pushes out. Over time the cells turn down their own production, so the baseline drops. That is the withdrawal side of it. Its not a separate bug.

At parties I always noticed how people talk about a substance as if it should be a clean pleasure switch on switch off. But the switch leaves a mark. Your body adjusts to the drug the way it adjusts to cold weather or bad sleep. The brain recalibrates to a new set point, which is why the first high feels great and repeated use feels weaker unless you take more.

A lot of the “adverse effects” people complain about are just the system trying to hold on. For a stimulant like coke, your heart, blood pressure and sleep all get dragged along with the pleasure. You dont get the jolt without the heart beating harder and the sleep getting wrecked. And yes, the standing leg thing is a separate issue that shows up in lots of skaters after long sessions, not specifically caused by the drugs.

So if you wanted a drug that gives you the same buzz but does nothing else, you basically need to build a molecule that fires only the “pleasure” circuit without touching anything else. In practice almost every drug pulls on several knobs at once. The more intense the euphoria, the deeper the compensation. Zero adverse effects would mean no tolerance buildup, no withdrawal, no heart or sleep disruption. That is a much tighter design target than most molecules can hit.

I can believe there could be some safer variants, and a few modern compounds are less brutal than old street drugs. But they are still not zero side effects. They are usually less toxic or have different dependence patterns. Its a spectrum, not an on-off thing.

The flat take is this: a drug with strong pleasure and truly zero downsides is a better goal than what most people get, but its still a very high bar. The body always notices, even if it takes weeks or months to show. If someone tells you a new “clean” pill can give you a high without any cost, I would want to see what happens to sleep, appetite and heart rate before believing it.

Ha, classic. The 3-in-1 thing is a compromise formula, not three products shoved into one bottle. It works because they dilute the washing and the conditioning so neither is really doing its job properly. My take is you get a thin wash with a film on top, and thats why some of the cheap ones feel waxy.

The 2-in-1 is different because its centered around conditioning, so it tends to be heavier and you dont get much scrubbing. The 3-in-1 is basically a thin wash with a light conditioning coat over it, and its what you reach for when you want one bottle but arent going to complain about it. As far as I know, the individual products just do one job without having to split its strength.

I would say the 3-in-1 is fine if you dont care about a good wash, but if you want your hair cleaned properly its not the one to use.

cheers
Dan

Hey Tom,

Good question. It's not like you can stand on the coast and watch the ground sliding. What actually happens is you use GPS.

You put a bunch of survey points on the ground, let the satellites pin their positions, then look at the change over months and years. That gives you how fast the spot moved, in millimeters per year. That number is tiny, so it takes a long time to be obvious.

I guess the trick is you have to compare different points against each other, because the whole Earth wobbles, so you need a reference. And the fastest movement is near the plate boundaries — where plates grind together or pull apart.

I noticed this last weekend out skating: GPS was giving me my speed instantly, but for a continent you're not looking at instantaneous speed, you're integrating tiny motions. I could be wrong, but I think the same satellites are used for both, which is why it works.

Also, they use lots of stations to get reliable numbers, and you need to know where a point is before you can measure change. If you want, I'll dig up the actual mm/year figures for the plate I'm curious about.

Cheers,
Dan

Hey, welcome to the team. You asked why inbreeding can mean a lower IQ, and it boils down to how we carry gene variants. Most people have one or two copies of mutations that only cause problems when you have them on both chromosomes. Because inbreeding pulls identical genes from related parents into the same child, the odds of those recessive defects showing up jump. That usually shows up as slightly lower cognitive scores, often cited around 15 IQ points below the general population average. And yeah, its definitely not a death sentence. Some families in small communities deal with it by keeping the family pool wide, which is a fair point. I guess the takeaway for you is that its the rare combinations of mutations that do the damage, not some single "bad gene."

It usually feels less painful because a lot of arm injuries hit areas with fewer nerve endings, especially the upper arm and elbow. The forearm has more sensitive spots, but still not quite as many as your trunk, hands, or face. So a graze or shallow hit there often feels less than the same thing to your belly or knuckles.

People overthink "why" and start comparing hits to other body parts, but the main thing that changes how bad it feels is what got hit, not what the word says it should hurt. A bullet or knife near a joint is a different story than on the bicep (which is why the hand matters too).

Ive had colleagues who said "my arm was shot" then acted like the world ended, when all that happened was a small graze near the elbow. The injury type matters, but so does the exact spot and how deep it goes.

The short answer is that CO is poisonous to breathe while CO2 mostly just makes you tired or short of breath, because CO2 is your own waste gas and CO is an almost invisible gas that grabs the oxygen-carrying part of your blood.

Your blood carries oxygen using hemoglobin, a protein inside red blood cells. Oxygen binds to hemoglobin reversibly, which is normal. Carbon monoxide, though, binds about two hundred times more strongly. I could be wrong on the exact multiple, but the scale is huge. One molecule of CO latches on and it is not easy for oxygen to push it off. So a few breaths in an enclosed space, especially near a generator or a car engine, can quietly fill a significant share of your hemoglobin.

CO is dangerous because it is colorless, has almost no smell, and it can drop your effective oxygen level before you notice. A common early sign is a mild headache or foggy head, and later symptoms include dizziness and nausea. With CO2, the issue is different. You exhale CO2 constantly, and the body manages it through your breathing and kidneys. High CO2 in a room makes you take deeper, faster breaths and feel exhausted or foggy, but that is a familiar signal. It is much less sneaky than CO, which is what makes it so nasty.

And CO2 alone is not poison to the same degree. It only becomes a problem in large quantities or when you are trapped in a tiny space with poor air exchange.

I would say the practical take is this: carbon dioxide is your own exhaust, whereas carbon monoxide is an intruder that outcompetes oxygen on your blood's oxygen carrier. You can live with normal CO2, but not with enough CO to displace oxygen in your bloodstream.

When an aircraft is going down or taking a big jolt, the brace position is about controlling where your body ends up during the deceleration. In the brace you sit as low in the seat as possible, keep your face down toward your knees, and hold on to something fixed in the cabin so you don't go flying. The reason this helps is that most passenger injuries come from being thrown into hard surfaces or loose objects, and from limbs striking the floor or seats. Keeping your head down and arms held in front of your chest means a head strike is less likely, and your arms can shield your face if something does come at you.

As far as I know, crews get trained to shout the calls in a way that makes you react fast and hold on with both hands. I guess the exact command may change with the airline, but the idea is the same: stay low, stay anchored, protect your head and neck.

Most of the businesses from before the Industrial Revolution just died with their owners, which is why no familiar brand from those days has stuck around. Crafters and merchants were the main players back then, and their names lived only as long as the people running them. A shop might operate for decades, but once the founder retired or passed, successors often rebranded or dissolved the business, so the original identity faded.

A handful of pre-industrial companies still make appearances in later industries, but that is not the same as surviving straight through every era. Most old brands were tied to specific places, families, or guilds, and when those social ties ended, the names went with them. In short, continuity was the missing ingredient, not product quality.

I know it looks backwards. The dealer quotes you a rate that sounds better than the bank, and everyone assumes that means the loan itself is cheaper. It isn’t. The rate is only one piece, and the dealer controls the rest.

The first thing they touch is the principal. A bank lends you the amount you negotiated. A dealership can take that number and quietly make it bigger. They’ll roll fees into the loan, or use a lower vehicle price that lets them inflate the financed amount to cover their own margin. That extra money is charged interest for years, and the lower rate doesn’t fix it because the base number is off.

I saw this when my scooter broke down last month and I needed a cheap car, fast. The dealer gave me a rate under the bank’s, but the amount they financed was bigger than I asked for, and a “documentation fee” and a “market adjustment” were tacked on. That adjustment has no real basis I could find, but once it was in the numbers it looked official. When I took it to a local credit union, they quoted a slightly higher rate, but the principal was exactly what I wanted, and the only charge was a small loan fee. Over the full term, the bank’s total came out lower.

Dealerships make money on the loan itself, not just on the car. The financing desk treats the loan like a product. A lower rate sounds appealing and keeps you from asking questions. It also gives them room to add charges that a bank or credit union might not, because you are comparing the two side by side. The bank doesn’t have the same incentive to pad the principal or force optional packages into the amount.

You can fight them. Ask for the loan amount before you sign, and ask for an itemized breakdown of every fee. If the rate is low but the principal is too high, you can negotiate the amount down, or bring your own financing. That doesn’t mean the bank is always the winner; if the dealer is transparent and the math checks out, they can be fine. But when you’re comparing a lower rate against a higher one, look at the total cost, not the headline number. In my case, the bank saved me money simply because the principal stayed clean and there were no mystery charges. The dealer’s rate was a trap wrapped in a good number.

Ha, the patchwork mess of cannabis laws is a real headache. I mean, weed is fully legal in places like California or Colorado, but its still technically a controlled substance federally. That federal-state tension is what makes this whole thing so confusing for everyday skaters and others just trying to figure out what’s okay on the weekend.

I think the current state of affairs is just... awkward. State laws keep changing, and the federal government hasn’t fully aligned with them yet. For people like me who hang out and roll up on weekends, it means you have to keep track of which state’s rules apply where you’re standing. Its not like you can just assume one rule fits everywhere.

I still think the trend is heading toward more legalization. States keep loosening their laws, and the feds are starting to act like they’ll follow. Its a slow move, but the direction is clear.

I used to think our bodies made lightning in miniature, and honestly that image stuck with me for years. I guess the truth is less dramatic. Nerve cells move charged particles called sodium and potassium ions across their outer membranes, which sets up a small electrical difference. Sodium flows in first, then potassium flows out, and that swap is what makes the signal move. That tiny voltage drop is what lets a signal zip down a nerve to a muscle. It is not a flash of electricity, more like a trickle, but enough to make a heartbeat or a finger flex.

How do musicians sample older songs?

First thing to know is that you don't just reach into a 1970s record and pull out a four-bar guitar riff. The song belongs to somebody, usually the label, and they want a cut or at least credit. In practice a lot of sampling is a negotiation: you pick the bit of audio you want, you get in touch with the label or the writer/performer representatives, you agree on money, and you get the sample in a clean audio file to drop into your project. Some labels are very generous about this, some are famously tight.

The actual music side is where the fun starts. You take a fragment, loop it, stretch it, reverse it, chop it into tiny slices. A four-second piano line can become a whole chorus. You might run it through a bitcrusher, add some distortion, quantise it, layer it under a drum break. The old song stops sounding like the original and becomes raw material.

People sometimes think old music is free. It is not, unless it has actually fallen into the public domain. A 1960s song may still have an active rights holder, and that rights holder controls the sample clearance. There have been famous fights over unlicensed samples, and the legal side of sampling is genuinely thorny.

What I personally find interesting is how the sample can completely recontextualise an old record. A folk melody, played on a 909 and chopped to bits, feels like something else entirely. Or take that 45rpm record, loop the vinyl crackle, and use it as texture under a hip-hop beat. The music gets a new life without the original songwriter even knowing.

For the actual workflow, most of my production friends work in a DAW. You drag a clip in, edit the in/out points, apply effects, and then you have a usable loop. The tricky part is finding the original record or a high-quality digital copy, and then negotiating the deal. Some artists pay a one-off fee, some pay royalties on every sale. The difference matters when a record takes off.

I'm not a lawyer, and I've been wrong about sampling law before, so treat the legal bit as a practical rule of thumb: if you're going to release the track commercially, you need permission and money, and the label usually says whether it's a flat fee or a royalty.

I still think sampling is one of the most creative ways to make new music, but you have to respect the people who made the original.

I keep wondering why my head hurts when I get a headache. I guess the pain isn’t coming from the bone, but from the pressure building up inside the skull, especially around the temples and behind my eyes. As far as I know, when you’re stressed or haven’t slept well, that pressure gets worse, and the tightness spreads. The part I care about is that squeezing feeling. My old pipes taught me that blocked systems pressurize; my head works the same way. I could be wrong, but stress and a bad night of sleep always seem to make it worse. I don’t like when I need painkillers and it still doesn’t take the pressure down fast enough. Cold water on my forehead and a dark room help more than taking the pill first. I also find that if I power through, the pressure stays. I try not to ignore the first twinge.

We got there at 7:20 p.m. Sunday because we had a 10 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought dinner would be easy. We put our names on their digital waitlist, then went back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We stood around until 8:40 p.m., and only then did someone casually say we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15 p.m. Just two people, and they offered nothing. If a wait goes that far past payment, say it upfront so your night isn't wasted. The food never happened. Zero stars, if that were even an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and there was no line at all. Two people ended up paying about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going I thought the price would be about the same as a steakhouse. Afterward I learned the buffet cost a bit more than I expected.

Honestly I was disappointed that steak was not on the menu. At that price I expected at least a steak option. The meat choices were lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but I feel like you can find those at other Las Vegas buffets for much less.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are common at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I had not run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I did not want to start smashing shells and send pieces flying. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station did not seem especially distinctive. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I did not try any.

I would call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you are curious it is worth trying once, especially if there is no wait. But if the line is long, I would probably reconsider.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

I guess sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been to Vegas since I was a kid, and I’ve seen plenty of shows over the years. Le Rêve at the Wynn was one I finally got to see, and it was mixed. Actually, closer to “not great.”

The circular stage is the smart part. You look down on it, so most seats have a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Individual acts were strong, too, with the strength pieces, aerialists and divers. Those people are real athletes. But it kept reminding me of Cirque du Soleil. Not a rip-off exactly, just that if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen similar stuff, often with clearer storytelling.

That clarity is the problem. What’s the story? I still wasn’t sure. A dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a pile of pretty images thrown at you without the show saying what it was trying to mean. There was also too much going on at once, with too many performers and moments stacked together. A smaller, more controlled show would probably hit harder. It had that usual Vegas “more is better” feel.

One practical note: if you’re staying at the Wynn or Encore, they have a deal at $99 instead of the usual $125, which helps. Would I go back? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay to see it again. It was average aside from a few stunts. I wasn’t blown away, and I didn’t think anyone else was. A few of my friends did like it, though, so if you haven’t seen it, it’s worth a look. Just don’t expect to come out in a daze.

About two years ago we ordered two shirts for my dad from Rockmount Ranch Wear by phone. The rep’s handwriting caused the mix-up: she wrote a “7” that looked like a “1”, so our address 5407 became 5401. The people at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to get it back, but the package vanished and we only found out a few weeks later.

Then, while disputing that order, we placed another order for two more shirts. Rockmount wouldn’t refund the original pair. The owner was the one dealing with it at that point. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong door but said no refund unless the shirts came back, and added that we were partly at fault for not being friendly enough to the 5401 folks, who lived four doors away. In the end we disputed the first charge with the card company and got the credit.
